analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Northern Rockies federal land as wilderness, off-limits to logging, mining, and drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 60 House sponsors, all Democrats, but was never considered by the committee it was sent to and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently protected large areas of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, wildlife corridors, and recovery areas. Once land is designated wilderness, new road building, logging, mining, and oil and gas drilling are generally banned there. The bill also directed agencies to restore damaged wildlands and set up a panel of scientists to evaluate remaining roadless areas. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who hunt, fish, hike, and recreate on public land, along with communities that depend on clean water from protected headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, and other rivers. The bill's findings say protecting roadless lands also preserves habitat for threatened species like grizzly bears, wolves, and salmon, and creates restoration jobs for local businesses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, hunters, anglers, and rural tourism towns

how_it_helps.text: Designates specified National Forest, National Park, and Bureau of Land Management lands in five states as wilderness, which permanently bars new road construction, timber harvest, mining, and oil and gas development there.
Adds segments of rivers and creeks in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, protecting water quality and fisheries.

Creates biological connecting corridors between core ecosystems so wildlife can move and interbreed, and sets up wildland recovery areas where restoration work would be contracted to local businesses.
Prohibits new roads, logging, mining, or oil and gas leasing that would impair roadless lands in the region without another act of Congress, pending evaluation by a panel of independent scientists.

analysis.who_pays: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies lose access to land they could otherwise develop; counties that receive payments tied to timber harvests on federal land would see less logging activity; and some motorized recreation users would lose access to areas closed to vehicles under wilderness rules.

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation bans road building and motorized use, which would close some areas to off-road vehicles, snowmobiles, and mountain bikers who currently use them.

Ending timber harvest and development on designated lands could reduce jobs and tax and royalty revenue in rural, resource-dependent communities in the affected states, even as the bill argues restoration work would create alternative employment.
The bill was introduced by a New York representative and all 60 sponsors were from outside the region's delegations, so it lacked the local consensus that most successful wilderness bills build.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a large, permanent conservation gain — protecting headwaters, wildlife habitat, and recreation land across a five-state region — at the cost of foregone logging, mining, and drilling on those specific acres and reduced motorized access. The bill itself argues that protecting the land supports recreation economies and avoids below-cost timber sales that lose taxpayer money, but that case was never tested in a hearing. Its design, covering whole ecosystems across five states rather than a negotiated local compromise, made passage unlikely in a Congress where the sponsoring party did not control the House committee with jurisdiction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Federal Lands subcommittee for the rest of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it expired in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney of New York introduced the bill on April 25, 2017, with 11 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On May 2, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Federal Lands, the last action of any kind recorded on the bill.
The bill gathered 59 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and never advanced past the subcommittee stage; it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests, along with off-road vehicle users, kept the current level of access and development options on these federal lands, since no protections were enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Extractive industries kept access to the land

for.name: Carolyn B. Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act and recruited 59 cosponsors.

for.name: 59 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none advanced it beyond committee.

against.name: Rob Bishop
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never held a hearing or markup on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 60 House sponsors — the lead sponsor and 59 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill got no traction with the Republican majority that controlled the committee and the floor schedule.

industries.note: The bill bars timber harvest and new road construction on designated lands, ending logging access there. It frames this as stopping below-cost timber sales that lose taxpayer money while supporting recreation and restoration jobs instead.
Mining and oil and gas leasing that would impair the roadless character of protected lands would be prohibited without a new act of Congress, closing off development on millions of acres.
Permanent protection of hunting, fishing, and wilderness recreation areas supports the amenity economies the bill's findings say depend on intact landscapes and clean water.
Wilderness designation bars motorized use, closing areas currently open to off-road vehicles and snowmobiles.
